title: Katakana and foreign words
titleJp: カタカナと がいらいご
canDo: I can read the 46 basic katakana letters and their versions with ゛ and ゜.
I can tell シ × ツ and ソ × ン apart by the direction of the long stroke.
I can read words with ー and ッ, like コーヒー and サッカー, with the right length.
I can recognize katakana's new combinations (ティ, ファ, ウィ…) in words like パーティー and カフェ.
I can write my name and my city in katakana, following the usual adaptation patterns.

blocks.t: Warm-up: read the hiragana chart from lesson 00-1 aloud, as fast as you can
Point 4a: the katakana chart and the tricky letters, reading the examples aloud
Points 4b to 4d: ー, ッ, the new combinations and how foreign words become katakana
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + writing your name in katakana

skills: Reading hiragana, even slowly: katakana has the same sounds and the same chart.
Understanding mora, long vowels and small っ (lesson 00-1). They come back here as ー and ッ.

grammar.title: The katakana chart
grammar.gloss: the same sounds, with straight strokes
grammar.explanation:
Katakana has **exactly the same sounds** and the same chart as hiragana: 46 basic letters, the same marks ゛ and ゜, and the same combinations with small ャ, ュ and ョ (キャ, シュ, チョ…). Only the shapes change: they are straighter and more angular.
• ア イ ウ エ オ · カ キ ク ケ コ · サ シ ス セ ソ · タ チ ツ テ ト · ナ ニ ヌ ネ ノ
• ハ ヒ フ ヘ ホ · マ ミ ム メ モ · ヤ ユ ヨ · ラ リ ル レ ロ · ワ ヲ · ン
• Some look like their hiragana partner: カ/か, キ/き, セ/せ, ヘ/へ, モ/も, ヤ/や, リ/り. Use that to your advantage. ヲ almost never appears.
• **What it is for**: foreign words (カメラ, テレビ), most foreign place names and Western people's names (ブラジル, マリア) and, sometimes, sound effects or emphasis, a bit like italics in English.
• **The four tricky ones**: シ (shi) and ツ (tsu), ソ (so) and ン (n). In シ and ン, the long stroke goes **up**, from bottom to top. In ツ and ソ, it goes **down**, from top to bottom. The short strokes of シ sit one above the other, on the left; those of ツ sit side by side, along the top.
grammar.structure: same chart as hiragana · か → カ · し → シ · ん → ン

examples.en: TV · ビ has the ゛, just as in hiragana
Maria · a Western name: written in katakana

pitfalls: Swapping シ (shi) and ツ (tsu): シャツ (shirt) starts with シ and ends with ツ. Look at the long stroke: in シ, it goes up.
Swapping ソ (so) and ン (n): パソコン has both. パ・ソ・コ・ン: first the one whose stroke goes down (ソ), at the end the one whose stroke goes up (ン).
Mixing up ク (ku) and ワ (wa), and ス (su) and ヌ (nu). In ワ, the first stroke is a short upright line; in ク, it slants. In ヌ, the second stroke crosses the leg; in ス, it only sticks out to the right.
Writing foreign words in hiragana: ぶらじる ✗ → ブラジル ✓.
howToStudy: ヅオリンゴー → Kana → Kana Trail, now in katakana, one row at a time. Check the stroke order in Kana → Write. Katakana doesn't have to be as fast as hiragana before you move on: once you can read it, even slowly, the names and loanwords in every lesson will keep polishing it.
In your notebook, write シ ツ ソ ン four times each, saying the direction of the long stroke aloud: "up", "down".
Speaking: read this lesson's vocabulary aloud, first slowly and then to the beat of the moras.

grammar.title: ー and ッ
grammar.gloss: long vowels and pauses in katakana
grammar.explanation:
The two timing features you saw in hiragana appear in their own way in katakana.
• **ー (the long-vowel bar)** stretches the vowel before it by one more mora. Instead of repeating the vowel, as hiragana does (おかあさん), katakana uses ー: コーヒー = コ・ー・ヒ・ー, 4 moras. A long e too: hiragana usually writes it with い (せんせい), katakana simply with ー (ケーキ, cake). In vertical writing, the bar stands upright.
• **ビル (building) × ビール (beer)**: ー is the only difference.
• **Small ッ** works just like hiragana っ: one mora of pause, with a doubled consonant in romaji. サッカー (soccer), ネット (internet). The consonant is not said twice: your mouth gets ready for it, the air stops for one beat, and it is released on the next letter.
• **ー and ッ each add exactly one beat**: ハト (pigeon: a native word, but animal names are often written in katakana; 2 beats) · ハート (heart, 3) · ハット (hat, 3).
• In foreign words, ッ can come before sounds that almost never double in native Japanese words: ベッド (bed), バッグ (bag).
• There is no 100% fixed rule, but there are patterns: English "-er" and "-or" at the end of a word usually become ー (サッカー, コンピューター), and a short vowel before a final t, k, p, d, g, ch or sh usually gains ッ (ネット, ベッド, バッグ). Before a final s, l, m or n there is usually no ッ: バス (bus), ホテル, ペン (pen).
grammar.structure: ー = stretches the vowel before it (コーヒー) · ッ = pause, doubled consonant (サッカー)

examples.en: coffee · コ・ー・ヒ・ー, 4 moras
soccer · ッ and ー in the same word

pitfalls: Ignoring the ー: ビル (building) × ビール (beer). Ask for a ビル at a bar and you are asking for a building.
Using ー in native Japanese words: in standard writing, a hiragana long vowel is written with a letter (おかあさん, とうきょう). ー belongs to katakana.
Reading ッ as "tsu": サ・ツ・カ・ー ✗ → サ・ッ・カ・ー ✓. サッカー is "sakkā", 4 moras, with a pause: one k, held for a beat.
Forgetting the ッ when writing: ネト ✗ → ネット ✓.
howToStudy: Speaking (a rhythm drill adapted from Sakubi): say ハト · ハート · ハット, clapping 2 · 3 · 3. Then ビル and ビール: 2 × 3.
Tap 🔊 on コーヒー and サッカー and imitate them, holding the ー and the ッ pause for one full beat.
In your notebook, write 5 words with ー and 3 with ッ from this lesson's vocabulary.

grammar.title: New combinations: ティ, ファ, ウィ…
grammar.explanation:
To imitate foreign sounds, katakana creates combinations that ordinary hiragana doesn't use. The rule is like キャ: a full-size letter + a **small vowel** (ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ) = **one mora**.
• **ティ** (ti) and **ディ** (di): the "tee" and "dee" sounds, which basic Japanese lacks (it only has チ chi and ジ ji). パーティー (party).
• **ファ フィ フェ フォ**: the breathy フ (no teeth on the lip, just as with ふ) with any vowel. It sounds close to an English f. カフェ (café), フォーク (fork).
• **ウィ ウェ ウォ**: "w" with i, e and o. ハロウィン (Halloween), ウェブ (web).
• **シェ, ジェ, チェ**: "she", "je" and "che". チェック (check).
• **ヴ** tries to imitate the v, but many words simply use the バ row: "violin" usually appears as バイオリン, and sometimes as ヴァイオリン. In speech, both sound like b.
• Not every word uses the new combinations: older words kept the older adaptation. "Ticket" became チケット, with チ, not ティ.
grammar.structure: letter + small ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ = 1 mora · テ + ィ → ティ · フ + ァ → ファ · ウ + ィ → ウィ

examples.en: Halloween · ウィ is a single mora

pitfalls: Writing ティ with a full-size イ: テイ is two moras (te-i). The vowel must be small: ティ.
Mixing up ティ and チ: パーティー is "pātī", with a t. チ is "chi".
Assuming every foreign "ti" becomes ティ: チケット (ticket) uses チ. Learn each word's spelling as it is, without inventing.
Reading ファ as two beats, "fu-a": the small ァ merges with フ into one mora, "fa". カフェ is カ・フェ, 2 moras.
howToStudy: Speaking: read these in pairs, feeling the difference: ティ/チ, ファ/ハ, ウィ/イ.
In your notebook, copy the new combinations (ティ ディ ファ フィ フェ フォ ウィ ウェ ウォ シェ ジェ チェ) and write this lesson's examples next to them.
Tap 🔊 on the examples and repeat each one 3 times.

grammar.title: How English words become katakana
grammar.gloss: rebuilding a foreign word with Japanese moras
grammar.explanation:
Japanese syllables are almost all consonant + vowel, ending in a vowel (or in ン). So when a foreign word comes into Japanese, it is **rebuilt out of Japanese moras**. The main patterns:
• **A consonant with no vowel gets one**, usually u: "Brazil" → ブ・ラ・ジ・ル, "golf" → ゴルフ. After t and d, the added vowel is usually o: "test" → テスト, "bed" → ベッド. After ch and j it is i: "match" → マッチ, "bridge" → ブリッジ. Some older words also use i after k: "cake" → ケーキ, "steak" → ステーキ.
• **l and r both become the ラ row**, because Japanese doesn't tell them apart: "lemon" → レモン, "radio" → ラジオ.
• **th usually becomes the サ row**, or the ザ row when it is voiced: "three" → スリー, "mother" → マザー. **v** usually becomes the バ row (point 4c).
• **Long vowels often become ー**: "cake" → ケーキ, "Lucas" → ルーカス (you will also see ルカス). Not always: "Pedro" → ペドロ, "Maria" → マリア. The "-er" ending also becomes ー (point 4b).
• **Long words shrink**, usually keeping the first moras of each part ("personal computer" → パソコン, "smartphone" → スマホ), or only of the first part ("convenience store" → コンビニ).
• **Not every katakana word is English**: パン (bread) comes from Portuguese, アルバイト (part-time job) from German, and コーヒー arrived through Dutch.
• **Names** have no official spelling: what counts is sounding close to how the person says it (ペドロ, アナ, ジョン, エミリー). A ・ goes between a foreign first name and last name: マリア・サントス.
grammar.structure: foreign word → Japanese moras (ブ・ラ・ジ・ル) · l and r → ラ row · long vowels → ー · long words shrink (パソコン)

examples.en: Brazil · every consonant got a vowel: ブ・ラ・ジ・ル
São Paulo · a place name rebuilt in moras: サ・ン・パ・ウ・ロ; ン before パ sounds like "m" (lesson 00-1)

pitfalls: Inventing spellings for common words: they already have a fixed form (ブラジル, サッカー, コーヒー). Free adaptation is only for proper names, like yours.
Saying the English word inside a Japanese sentence: コーヒー is "kō-hī", not "coffee", and ホテル is "ho-te-ru", not "hotel". A Japanese listener may not recognize the English pronunciation.
Assuming a katakana word means exactly what the English word means: マンション is an apartment in a building, not a mansion.
Stressing one syllable: ブラジル is 4 equal moras, ブ・ラ・ジ・ル, not "bra-ZIL".
howToStudy: Write in katakana your name, your city and the names of 3 family members, following the patterns. Then compare with the homework model (h4).
Speaking: read ブラジル, サンパウロ and パソコン to the beat of the moras, with no stressed syllable.
Guessing game: take katakana words from Wagotabi or from packaging and try to work out the foreign word behind each one.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write katakana with straight strokes and check the stroke order in Kana → Write. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it in your next session.

tasks.prompt: Read each word aloud, write its romaji next to it, and work out the foreign word behind it.

items.note: From English "hotel": the final l became ル.
Two ー: コ・ー・ヒ・ー, 4 moras. It came from Dutch "koffie", close to English "coffee".
From "restaurant": the s got a vowel and became ス.
From "fork": フォ is a single mora, and the "or" became a long vowel.

tasks.prompt: シ, ツ, ソ or ン? Fill in the right letter (careful: one item is a trick).

items.note: シ at the start, ツ at the end: both in the same word.
ソ, whose long stroke goes down.
ン, whose long stroke goes up.
The trick: it's the small ッ, a pause — not a full-size ツ or シ.

tasks.prompt: Write these in katakana. All the words are in this lesson's vocabulary.

items.note: With ー. Without it, it becomes ビル (building).
ティ with a small ィ, and two ー. You will also see パーティ, without the last ー: that is also correct.
You will also see ハロウィーン, with ー.

tasks.prompt: Write your full name and the name of your city in katakana. Then read them aloud, to the beat of the moras, and record yourself.

items.note: Check: every consonant has a vowel (ス at the end), the r became ロ, and there is a ・ between the first and last name. Names have no official spelling: if it sounds close, it is right.
Check: place names usually come without ・ between their parts, and every syllable keeps a full vowel: リ・オ・デ・ジャ・ネ・イ・ロ.

workbook.tip: Do it once you can read all of katakana, even slowly.
After mastering the ア and カ rows on the Kana Trail.
After the サ and タ rows.
After the ナ and ハ rows.
After the マ and ヤ rows.
After the ラ and ワ rows and ン. Check it with the official Genki Answer Key.

practice.what: ヅオリンゴー → Kana → Kana Trail, in katakana: one new row per session, reviewing the earlier ones. Use Kana → Write for the stroke order of シ, ツ, ソ and ン.
Its mixed mode combines hiragana and katakana. If you swap シ and ツ, its confusion hunt records the pair and brings the look-alike back soon after; in its weaknesses tab you can drill that exact pair.
Play normally and look for katakana words in the menus and dialogues. Read 5 of them aloud, try to guess the foreign word behind each one, and note them in your notebook.

Turn on the Japanese keyboard (IME) that comes with your computer or phone and type 5 words from this lesson. You type in romaji and choose the katakana: ー is the hyphen key, ッ comes from doubling the consonant (netto → ネット), ティ is "thi" and ファ is "fa". On Windows, F7 turns what you just typed into katakana. Typing is a separate skill from reading, and you will need it for the app's Journal.

Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times, holding the ー and the ッ pause. Then say your name in katakana to the beat of the moras (ペ・ド・ロ) and record it. Listen: did it come out with no stressed syllable?

culture.title: Words Japanese borrowed from Portuguese
culture.titleJp: ポルトガルごから きた ことば
culture.body: The Portuguese were the first Europeans to reach Japan, around 1543, and they brought new products and new words. Some are still used today: **パン** (bread), **カステラ** (a sponge cake whose name comes from *Castela*, Portuguese for Castile), **タバコ** (tobacco, cigarettes; Portuguese *tabaco*), **ボタン** (button) and **カッパ** (a raincoat; Portuguese *capa*, "cape"). **てんぷら** is also widely thought to come from Portuguese, although the exact source word is still debated. Some of these words are so old that they no longer feel foreign: てんぷら, for example, is usually written with a kanji and hiragana (天ぷら), not in katakana. Beware of a famous myth: ありがとう does **not** come from the Portuguese word for "thank you". It is an old Japanese word, and the resemblance is a coincidence.
culture.try: Read these aloud, mora by mora: パ・ン, カ・ス・テ・ラ, タ・バ・コ, ボ・タ・ン, カ・ッ・パ. After each one, say what it means in English.

checklist: I can read the 46 basic katakana letters, with ゛ and ゜, without looking at the chart.
I can tell シ/ツ and ソ/ン apart by the direction of the long stroke, when reading and when writing.
I can read ー and ッ with the right length: ビル × ビール, サッカー.
I can read the new combinations (ティ, ファ, フォ, ウィ…) in words like パーティー and カフェ.
I can write my name and my city in katakana without looking at the patterns.
I can type katakana words with ー and ッ (コーヒー, サッカー) on a Japanese keyboard.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
